intro: In spoken British English, “have got” is the most common way to talk about things you own, your family, how people look, illnesses and appointments.
objectifs: Use “have got” in the present in positive sentences, negatives and questions, with short forms.
Give correct short answers (Yes, I have. / No, she hasn't.).
Use “have got” for possessions, family, appearance, health and plans in your diary.
Know when you can't use “have got” (actions, age, the past), and use “have / do you have”, which is more common in American English.

texte: “Have got” has two words: have (or has for he, she, it) + got. It simply means “have”: “got” doesn't add any idea of the past.
When we speak, we almost always use short forms: I've got, she's got. Be careful: “'s” can mean “is” (she's French) or “has” (she's got a car). The word “got” tells you that it means “has”.
sections.note: Only he / she / it changes: he / she / it HAS got. Never say “she have got”.

texte: Like “to be”, “have got” doesn't use “do”. For the negative, add not after have / has (haven't got, hasn't got). For a question, put have / has before the subject (Have you got…?).
In short answers, use only have / has, without got: Yes, I have. No, she hasn't. Like with “to be”, no short form after Yes: don't say “Yes, I've”.
exemples: Have you got a pen? — Yes, I have. Here you are.
A short answer, then you give the pen.
She hasn't got any brothers or sisters.
What have you got in your bag?

texte: Use “have got” for a situation, not an action: things you own, family and friends, how a person looks, illnesses, and plans in your diary.
exemples: Amina has got long black hair and brown eyes.
I've got a headache. / He's got a cold.
Sorry, I've got a meeting at three.
A common phrase at the end of a presentation.
sections.note: “Hair” (on your head) is uncountable and has no article: She's got long hair (not “a long hair” or “long hairs”).

texte: Don't use “have got” for actions. For breakfast, a shower, a good time or a party, use “have” alone: I have breakfast at seven, We have a party on Saturday. (You will see this “have” again with the present simple, lesson 6.)

Don't use it for age (I'm 20, not “I've got 20 years”) or in the past: in the past, just say “had” (I had a dog when I was a child). Don't use it after “to” or a modal either: say “You need to have a passport”, not “to have got”.

lignes: I had got a cat in 2010.

sections.titre: “Have got” or “have”? British and American English
texte: For possession, you can also use “have” alone, like a normal verb. Then it uses do / does in negatives and questions: I don't have a car. Do you have a car? — Yes, I do.

“Have got” is more common in spoken British English and a little informal. “Have” + do is normal in American English and also very common in the UK, especially in writing. Both are correct. Just don't mix them in one sentence: never say “Do you have got…?” or “Have you got…? — Yes, I do”.

lignes: Yes, she has. / No, she hasn't.
Yes, she does. / No, she doesn't.

sections.note: In informal American English, you also hear “I got a car” (without have). It is very informal: don't write it.

formule: I / you / we / they have got ('ve got) · he / she / it has got ('s got) · haven't / hasn't got · Have you got…? — Yes, I have.
prononciation: Short forms “I've got” /aɪv ɡɒt/ and “she's got” /ʃiːz ɡɒt/: the v and z are light but you must hear them, or it sounds like “I got”.
“got” is /ɡɒt/ in British English (short, open o) and /ɡɑːt/ in American English.
“haven't” /ˈhævnt/ and “hasn't” /ˈhæznt/: two syllables, stress on the first; the final t is often very light.
In a question, “have” is weak: Have you got…? /həv juː ɡɒt/. In a short answer, it is strong: Yes, I HAVE /hæv/.
Breathe out the h in “have” and “has”. Don't say “I 'ave”.
erreurs: She have got a car.
She has got a car. / She's got a car.
he / she / it: has.
Do you have got a pen?
Have you got a pen? / Do you have a pen?
Don't mix do and have got.
Have you got a car? — Yes, I've got.
Yes, I have.
Short answer: have / has alone, without got.
I've got 30 years.
Age uses “to be”.
I've got a shower every morning.
I have a shower every morning.
Action → have alone, not have got.
She's got blue eye and a long hair.
She's got blue eyes and long hair.
Eyes is plural; hair is uncountable, no a.
I don't have got a bike.
I haven't got a bike. / I don't have a bike.
The negative of have got is haven't got.

dialogue.contexte: Two neighbours talk on the stairs of a building in Liège. One of them is new.
lignes: Hi! I'm Chloé, your new neighbour. Have you got a minute?
A polite question with have got.
Sure. Welcome! Have you got everything for the flat?
Almost. But I haven't got a drill. Have you got one?
Yes, I have. I can bring it tonight. Have you got children?
Yes, I've got a son. He's six. And he's got a very noisy dog!
No problem. We've got a cat, so they can be friends.
Great. Oh, sorry, I've got an appointment at five. See you later!
Have got for a plan in your diary.

a device to call and send messages

I've got an appointment at the dentist's.

items: Has the hotel got a pool? (no)

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Correct it.
items: We've got lunch at one o'clock.
We have lunch at one o'clock.
Do you have got a pen?
Have you got a pen? / Do you have a pen?

exercices.consigne: Rewrite the sentence with “have got” (short form).
items: We have a meeting at ten.
We've got a meeting at ten.

exercices.consigne: Write four true sentences with “have got”: something you have, something you haven't got, your family, and how you look (hair, eyes).
items: I've got a laptop but I haven't got a car. I've got two brothers and a sister. I've got short brown hair and dark eyes.

a_retenir: I / you / we / they've got · he / she / it's got (= has got).
Negative: haven't got / hasn't got. Question: Have you got…? Has she got…?
Short answer without got: Yes, I have. / No, she hasn't.
For possessions and states, never for actions (I have breakfast), age (I'm 25) or the past (I had).
The same idea with do: Do you have…? — Yes, I do. Don't mix the two.
